source: the relations of the third confirmatory batch, specified from publisher documentation (e3/truth/docs/fresh3/) by three subagents that never saw data, mined FDs or model answers; parts A (TPC-C, Epinions, Twitter, Synthea), B (HGNC, GLEIF, ONSPD, FEC, OurAirports), C (NPPES, Companies House, Open Payments, Stack Exchange)
rule: part A: part A: Sigma* is the set of FDs that the publisher documentation implies among the attributes of each relation, projected and closed over the dropped columns, each with a verbatim quote; sure when the quoted text states it (a declared primary key, unique constraint or foreign key to a declared key in the pinned DDL, a ':key:' row or a 'Foreign key to' row of the Synthea data dictionary), unsure when it needs an inference the text does not spell out. For the three BenchBase benchmarks the DDL at the pinned commit is the specification of the generated data (scale factor 1, loaded and never executed); a dependency that the TPC-C specification or the OLTP-Bench paper states and the DDL neither declares nor contradicts is recorded with sure: false, quoting both; the TPC-C population rules (clause 4.3.3.1) make the warehouse ids and several other columns constant at one warehouse, and these constants are dropped as rule 1 asks, the declared keys being projected onto the kept columns with both quotes (a projected key stays sure, since a key minus a documented constant is a key, and key is null because the declared key is not wholly among the attributes); a root without a declared key keeps key null and only the foreign-key dependencies. For Synthea the CSV File Data Dictionary is the specification. Dependencies the documentation hints at but does not state (code -> description, random strings that happen to be unique, accidental equalities of generated data, counts and conditional constants) are listed under undocumented_regularities and are not part of Sigma*. Written from the documentation alone, before any data file was opened. part B: Sigma* is the set of FDs that the publisher documentation implies among the attributes of each relation, projected and closed over the dropped columns, each with a verbatim quote (file name and section or page) and a one-sentence justification; sure when the quoted text states it (a declared key or unique identifier of the root such as 'list each LEI only once', 'one record for each candidate', 'Unique link ID' or 'the actual internal OurAirports primary key is id', a foreign key or look-up reference to a table with a declared key, an allocation 'via lookup' from one geography to another, a stated derivation of one column from another, a stated containment such as 'each consists of a grouping of OAs'); unsure when it needs an inference the text does not spell out (a country read off a per-country code range, a nesting stated in the past tense or for another vintage, a copy of a master's value in a linkage file), when the text is ambiguous, or when the left-hand side can be empty or unresolved (an optional ISO 3166-2 region, a reserved ELF code, a dangling look-up) so that the dependency holds among non-empty values only. Plausible, common-knowledge or value-level implications (ISSUED implies ACTIVE, a ZIP code implies a state) and documented non-dependencies (a pseudo code shared by every district of a country, a gps_code 'not guaranteed to be globally unique', 'the same frequency may appear multiple times for an airport') are listed under undocumented_regularities and are not part of Sigma*. Columns are named exactly as the documentation spells them (GLEIF: the Golden Copy CSV element paths of the Data Dictionary; ONSPD: the field names of Annex A of the August 2026 user guide; FEC: the header files; OurAirports and HGNC: the dictionary / archive page); where two tables share a name the looked-up column is prefixed (CN_, CM_, airport_, region_, country_). Many-to-one joins only, along keys the documentation declares; one relation per documented root table, named fresh3_<source>_<root> where a source has several; the GLEIF code lists were not written because their CSV headers are undocumented and the ELF code is not a row key of the ELF list. Written from the documentation alone, before any data file was opened. part C: Sigma* is the set of FDs that the publisher documentation implies among the attributes of each relation, projected and closed over the dropped columns, each with a verbatim quote naming the file and the section or page; sure when the quoted text states it (a declared key or unique identifier of the root, a declared unique identifier of an entity determining that entity's other documented attributes, a foreign key or link to a table with a declared key; a table that the schema documentation marks as the parent table of foreign keys that reference it by its Id counts as having Id declared), unsure when it needs an inference the text does not spell out (the justification says which); both directions of an identifier pair get the same standard. Plausible or common-knowledge dependencies (postal geography, company law, one profile per NPI, one badge class per badge name), documented conditional-emptiness statements and documented non-dependencies are listed under undocumented_regularities and are not part of Sigma*. A relation whose documentation declares no key of the root gets key null (the NPPES reference files, whose rows are 'associated with an NPI record' without a declared key of their own; Stack Exchange Comments, Votes, Badges, PostHistory, whose Id FD is kept with sure false), so that item 61 (b) 2 can exclude it by rule. Relations have at most 25 attributes, many-to-one joins only along keys the documentation declares (a file in two roles is two tables), columns named exactly as the documentation spells them, and no person name, street address, telephone, e-mail or licence number. Written from the documentation alone, before any data file was opened.

truth.clause: onspd_user_guide/ONSPD User Guide Aug 2026.pdf, p. 31, Annex A 'ONSPD Record Specification', field PCD7: "Unit postcode - 7 character version", "All current ('live') postcodes within the United Kingdom, the Channel Islands and the Isle of Man, received monthly from Royal Mail. Also, all terminated ('closed') postcodes that have not been subsequently re-used by Royal Mail within the United Kingdom and by the postal administrations in the Channel Islands and the Isle of Man."; onspd_user_guide/ONSPD User Guide Aug 2026.pdf, p. 9, section 12 'Terminated Postcodes': "If, and when, a postcode is subsequently re-used by Royal Mail the old grid reference and termination date are removed, thus deleting all reference to the former existence of the postcode from the ONSPD."; onspd_user_guide/ONSPD User Guide Aug 2026.pdf, p. 6, section 6: "Postcodes are always assigned to single administrative and electoral areas based upon a single grid reference"
truth.justification: The directory holds one record per unit postcode (a re-used postcode replaces its former record rather than adding one) and each postcode is assigned to single areas, so the postcode determines every field of its record and the names looked up from them.

audit.quote: Unit postcode – 7 character version ‖ All current (‘live’) postcodes within the United Kingdom, the Channel Islands and the Isle of Man, received monthly from Royal Mail. Also, all terminated (‘closed’) postcodes that have not been subsequently re-used by Royal Mail within the United Kingdom and by the postal administrations in the Channel Islands and the Isle of Man. ‖ The most recent occurrence of the postcode’s date of introduction. ‖ If, and when, a postcode is subsequently re-used by Royal Mail the old grid reference and termination date are removed, thus deleting all reference to the former existence of the postcode from the ONSPD. ‖ Postcodes are always assigned to single administrative and electoral areas based upon a single grid reference (which is the mean of all the addresses in the postcode, snapped to the address closest to the mean). ‖ Lookup files linking these codes to statutory area names are included with the ONSPD, in the 'Documents' folder. ‖ The names of all administrative and health areas are the standard names adopted for use throughout National Statistics. The names are those used in Acts of Parliament and Statutory Instruments to publish changes to the administrative and health geographies.

truth.clause: onspd_user_guide/ONSPD User Guide Aug 2026.pdf, p. 43, Annex A, field OA11CD: "The 2011 Census OAs in GB and SAs in Northern Ireland were based on 2001 Census OAs, and they form the building bricks for defining higher level geographies."; onspd_user_guide/ONSPD User Guide Aug 2026.pdf, p. 17, section 33: "The Lower Layer SOAs (LSOA) were designed with a mean population figure of 1,500 and each consists of a grouping of OAs, typically five." and "DZs are groups of OAs which have populations of between 500 and 1,000 household residents."; onspd_user_guide/ONSPD User Guide Aug 2026.pdf, p. 18, section 38: "Postcodes have been assigned to the urban or rural category of the OA into which each one falls."; onspd_user_guide/ONSPD User Guide Aug 2026.pdf, p. 45, Annex A, field OAC11IND: "The 2011 Census OAC code for each postcode in the UK." with p. 16, section 32: "The 2011 Census OAC is used to group together geographic areas according to key characteristics common to the population in that grouping."; onspd_user_guide/ONSPD User Guide Aug 2026.pdf, p. 53, Annex E 'Geography Allocation Diagram': "This diagram shows the data supplied to ONS through the Gridlink process from Royal Mail and Ordnance Surevy (OS), and the methodology for adding each geography to the ONSPD - either via lookup or via a digital point in polygon (PIP) process.", Lookup column: "SOA (from OA)", "Rural/urban indicator (from OA)", "Output Area Classification (from OA)", "Rural Urban Classification (from OA)", "IMD (from OA)"
truth.justification: The 2011 OA is the building brick of the higher geographies: LSOAs/DZs are groupings of OAs, the rural-urban class and the OAC are properties of the OA, and Annex E allocates SOA, rural/urban indicator, OAC and IMD by lookup from the OA, so the OA determines them; MSOA, TTWA, SICBL and ICB follow through the LSOA (next entries).

audit.quote: This diagram shows the data supplied to ONS through the Gridlink process from Royal Mail and Ordnance Surevy (OS), and the methodology for adding each geography to the ONSPD – either via lookup or via a digital point in polygon (PIP) process. ‖ Lookup: SOA (from OA) ‖ Rural/urban indicator (from OA) ‖ Country (from LAD) ‖ SSR (from LAD) ‖ CAS ward (from OA) ‖ Output Area Classification (from OA) ‖ NI Primary Care area (from ward) ‖ ITL (from OA) ‖ Rural Urban Classification (from OA) ‖ SICBL (from LSOA) ‖ TTWA (from LSOA) ‖ PFA (from LAD) ‖ IMD (from OA) ‖ Cancer Alliance (from SICBL) ‖ ICB (from SICBL) ‖ The 2011 Census OAs in GB and SAs in Northern Ireland were based on 2001 Census OAs, and they form the building bricks for defining higher level geographies. ‖ The Lower Layer SOAs (LSOA) were designed with a mean population figure of 1,500 and each consists of a grouping of OAs, typically five. ‖ DZs are groups of OAs which have populations of between 500 and 1,000 household residents. ‖ Postcodes have been assigned to the urban or rural category of the OA into which each one falls. ‖ OAs have been assigned to the urban or rural category on an individual basis, based upon data received from GROS. ‖ The 2011 Census OAC code for each postcode in the UK. ‖ The 2011 Census OAC is used to group together geographic areas according to key characteristics common to the population in that grouping. These groupings are called clusters and are derived using 2011 population census data. ‖ The IMD rank for the 2011 LSOA (or OA or DZ) of each postcode, where 1 is the most deprived. A zero is included for Channel Islands and Isle of Man, also for postcodes with no grid reference. ‖ The 228 current TTWAs were defined in 2015 using 2011 Census information on home and work addresses and are built from 2011 Census LSOAs in England and Wales, data zones in Scotland, and SOAs in Northern Ireland (see Section 34). ‖ They came into effect on 1 April 2013 and were built from 2011 LSOAs. In July 2022 they were renamed to Sub ICB (Integrated Care Board) Locations as part of the STP/ICB changes (see also Section 44). ‖ The ICB code for each postcode. Pseudo codes are included for Wales, Scotland, Northern Ireland, Channel Islands and Isle of Man. The field will otherwise be blank for postcodes with no grid reference.

Pseudo codes are included for Northern Ireland, Channel Islands and Isle of Man. ‖ The IMD rank for the 2011 LSOA (or OA or DZ) of each postcode, where 1 is the most deprived. In July 2022 they were renamed to Sub ICB (Integrated Care Board) Locations as part of the STP/ICB changes (see also Section 44). ‖ This diagram shows the data supplied to ONS through the Gridlink process from Royal Mail and Ordnance Surevy (OS), and the methodology for adding each geography to the ONSPD – either via lookup or via a digital point in polygon (PIP) process. ‖ Lookup: SOA (from OA) ‖ Rural/urban indicator (from OA) ‖ Country (from LAD) ‖ SSR (from LAD) ‖ CAS ward (from OA) ‖ Output Area Classification (from OA) ‖ NI Primary Care area (from ward) ‖ ITL (from OA) ‖ Rural Urban Classification (from OA) ‖ SICBL (from LSOA) ‖ TTWA (from LSOA) ‖ PFA (from LAD) ‖ IMD (from OA) ‖ Cancer Alliance (from SICBL) ‖ ICB (from SICBL)
